sum: The ice is advancing, invading armies threaten the empire, and the last hope for Abeth may lie in ancient artefacts of power. Nona, now on the threshold of becoming a full sister, must make her final choices about loyalty and sacrifice as the story moves between two timelines and her friends scatter on desperate missions across a dying world.
bg: Mark Lawrence published Holy Sister in 2019 to complete the Book of the Ancestor trilogy. He later returned to the same world, Abeth, in the Book of the Ice trilogy, beginning with The Girl and the Stars in 2020, which can be read independently.
br: Read only after Red Sister and Grey Sister; this profile avoids their revelations. As in the earlier books, two timelines alternate before converging. A quick recap of book two is helpful before starting.
la: Lawrence brings the trilogy’s action, friendships and mysteries to a climax, with a focus on Nona’s inner life and the bonds she has made, balancing battle with quieter moments of grief and humour.
cx: The conclusion reveals more of Abeth’s science-fiction backstory, while staying centred on character rather than lore. Lore never overwhelms the friendships at its centre. Its revelations reframe the earlier books without undoing them.
th: Sacrifice
Saving others may cost Nona everything she has fought to keep.
Friendship
The friendships of the convent are the trilogy’s emotional heart.
Hope against the ice
Even on a dying world, people choose to fight for a future.
fit: Completes a quick, propulsive trilogy with a strong emotional ending. Its final chapters are both exciting and moving.
mis: The dual timeline can feel fragmented, and the ending may feel abrupt to some.
rq: What final choice does Nona face?
What does the ending reveal about Abeth?
dq: What does it say about friendship?

sum: Logen Ninefingers, a notorious barbarian warrior tired of killing, survives one fight too many and is summoned south by an ancient wizard. Glokta, a crippled former war hero, now works as a torturer for the Inquisition and hates every minute. Jezal, a vain young nobleman, wants only to win a fencing contest. As war looms on two fronts, their paths begin to converge.
bg: Joe Abercrombie published The Blade Itself in 2006 as the first of the First Law trilogy. It helped define grimdark fantasy, which favours morally grey characters and dark humour over heroic quests. Abercrombie had worked as a freelance film editor.
br: The first book is mostly character introduction and set-up, with the main plot gathering pace slowly. The pleasure lies in the voices, especially Glokta’s bitter internal monologue. Chapters rotate among several viewpoints.
la: Abercrombie writes in close third person with distinct voices, sharp dialogue and black humour, and deliberately subverts fantasy tropes of wise wizards, noble heroes and glorious war. Readers often laugh and wince on the same page.
cx: The trilogy is a response to traditional epic fantasy in the Tolkien mould, asking what violence, power and war really do to people. It is also a book about trauma, disability and survival.
th: Violence and its cost
Violence corrupts, haunts and diminishes those who use it.
Can people change?
Characters struggle against what they have already become.
Power and manipulation
The powerful use others as pieces in their own long games.
fit: A darkly funny, completed trilogy that contrasts sharply with the more hopeful fantasy on your list.
mis: Graphic violence, torture and cynicism may not suit every reader, and the first book is slow on plot.
rq: Which character’s voice do you enjoy most?
How does Abercrombie subvert fantasy tropes?
dq: Can people truly change in this world?
Is grimdark more realistic or just more cynical?

sum: The war widens. Glokta is sent to defend a besieged city in the south, where treachery is everywhere. Colonel West struggles to hold together a disastrous northern campaign under an incompetent prince. Logen, Jezal and a few others follow the wizard Bayaz on a long, dangerous quest to the edge of the world for a mysterious artefact.
bg: Joe Abercrombie published Before They Are Hanged in 2007 as the middle volume of the First Law trilogy, widely regarded as one of the strongest middle books in modern fantasy. Its quest storyline in particular plays with classic fantasy expectations.
br: Read after The Blade Itself; this profile avoids its developments. Three storylines alternate, each with its own tone: siege thriller, war story and road-trip quest. Glokta’s siege chapters are especially gripping.
la: Abercrombie deepens characterisation and dark humour, showing characters changing under pressure, and keeps undermining expectations of heroism and quests. Each storyline has its own rhythm, and the cross-cutting builds tension across the whole book.
cx: The book’s title comes from a line attributed to Heinrich Heine: we should forgive our enemies, but not before they are hanged. That bitter wit sets the tone for the volume.
th: Duty and survival
Glokta and West try to do their duty in impossible situations.
Friendship in adversity
Unlikely bonds form on the quest between people who dislike each other.
Futility of war
Leaders’ vanity and incompetence cost ordinary soldiers their lives.
fit: Continues the trilogy with stronger plot momentum and character growth. Its pacing is the best of the trilogy.
mis: Violence and bleakness continue, and the quest storyline subverts expectations in ways some may find frustrating.
rq: How does Glokta handle the siege?
What is the quest really for?
dq: Who is the most changed character?

sum: Wars converge on the capital, and every character must face the consequences of choices made across the trilogy. Logen returns north to settle old scores, Jezal finds himself in a role he never wanted, Glokta is squeezed between powerful masters, and the true games of the trilogy’s powerful figures are finally revealed.
bg: Joe Abercrombie published Last Argument of Kings in 2008 to complete the First Law trilogy. He has since written standalone novels and a second trilogy set in the same world. The original trilogy remains the best place to start.
br: Read only after the first two books; this profile avoids their revelations. The ending is deliberately unconventional, so resist expecting a classic triumphant finale. Expect several long battle sequences.
la: Abercrombie brings the storylines together in large battles and political reversals, while keeping the focus on character and on uncomfortable truths about power. Its final chapters reward attention to everything said earlier.
cx: The title comes from the phrase engraved on French cannons under Louis XIV, ultima ratio regum, the last argument of kings. Abercrombie takes every chapter title and epigraph seriously.
th: Power
Behind every throne and title someone else is pulling strings.
Change
Characters struggle, and often fail, to escape their own natures.
War’s cost
Victory and defeat both leave ruins behind them.
fit: Completes the trilogy with a bold, memorable ending. Readers who enjoy moral complexity will find it memorable.
mis: The bleak, subversive ending may disappoint readers wanting justice or heroism. It offers little comfort.
rq: What does each character finally become?
How does the ending subvert expectations?
dq: Is the ending satisfying or deliberately unsatisfying?
What does the trilogy say about power?

sum: Maia, the half-goblin youngest son of the elven emperor, has grown up exiled and unloved on a remote estate. When his father and elder brothers die in an airship explosion, he unexpectedly inherits the throne. Untrained, shy and surrounded by courtiers who despise him, he must learn to rule, find allies, and uncover who caused the crash, all while staying kind.
bg: Katherine Addison, the pen name of Sarah Monette, published the novel in 2014. It won the Locus Award for Best Fantasy Novel and has become a beloved example of hopeful, gentle fantasy. Addison later wrote related books set in the same world.
br: The opening is dense with invented names, titles and formal forms of address; a glossary at the back helps. Let the court’s etiquette become familiar gradually. The formal register is part of the charm.
la: Addison focuses on court politics, etiquette and Maia’s inner life rather than battles, building tension from conversations and small acts of courage and kindness. Small gestures of courtesy carry great weight.
cx: The book belongs to a strand sometimes called hopepunk or cosy fantasy, emphasising decency and compassion as political acts. It shows that fantasy can be gripping without battles or villains in every chapter.
th: Kindness as strength
Maia’s simple decency is his most radical political act.
Belonging
An outsider must make a home among people who reject him.
Power and responsibility
Ruling well means caring about ordinary people the court ignores.
fit: A warm, hopeful counterpoint to the grimdark fantasy on your list. It is a comfort read with real depth.
mis: Slow pacing, complex names and lack of action may frustrate some readers. Very little happens in conventional terms.
cw: Childhood abuse and neglect in backstory.
rq: How does Maia’s past shape his rule?
How does Addison build tension without battles?
dq: Is kindness a realistic political strategy?
How does the book compare with grimdark fantasy?
